title: From Maps to Analysis
text:
The goal of this workshop series is to provide a gentle introduction to creating maps and conducting geospatial analysis without the need to have programming skills.
We have organized this curriculum into three workshops:

title: From Maps to Analysis
section: Workshop 1 - I want to make a map
text:
Workshop 1 - I want to make a map
3-hour workshop using ArcGIS Online to create a map. This workshop will introduce the basic elements of a map and leverage ArcGIS Online to learn how to:

adjust the background basemap
add an existing data layer to a map
change symbology of vector data
draw lines and polygons on a map

The workshop ends with exporting a map suitable for inclusion in a publication.

title: From Maps to Analysis
text:
Workshop 2 - Working with data
3-hour workshop using ArcGIS Online to conduct basic GIS data exploration and visualization.

more about vector data
raster data
Living Atlas data
data import & export

title: From Maps to Analysis
text:
Workshop 3 - Geospatial analysis
4-hour workshop. A Carpentry-like, hands-on session introducing the analytical features of ArcGIS Online versus Pro on a Windows desktop.
This session will introduce the learner to the differences between Online and Pro. We will cover topics such as:

raster calculation
buffering
interpolation
zonal statistics

title: I want to make a map
text:
The goal of this lesson is to demonstrate how to make a simple map, suitable for inclusion in a publication, using ArcGIS Online. As an exercise, you will be creating a map of the UCSB campus bicycle infrastructure and proposing a campus access improvement. We will follow a typical workflow of:
As we will describe under Other approaches at the end of this lesson, there are many tools and techniques that can be used to create such a map. An advantage of using a GIS tool such as ArcGIS Online, and the central motivation for using GIS in this lesson, is that a GIS tool allows map elements to be interpreted and manipulated as data, and in this way spatial analysis becomes possible.
ArcGIS Online is but one of many GIS tools in existence. We use it in this lesson because it is in wide use in both commercial and academic settings. However, it is important to recognize that it is a proprietary and closed system that requires a paid subscription to use. We note limitations and ramifications of using ArcGIS Online on the reproducibility and citability of one’s work under Caveats of using ArcGIS Online at the end of this lesson.

title: I want to make a map
text:
Log on to ArcGIS Online
https://ucsb.maps.arcgis.com
Sign on with your UCSB NetID. You may need to enter “ucsb” into the url box. Do not use the ArcGIS login! This is for users who do NOT have a UCSB NetID.






Figure 2: ArcGIS Online login page for UCSB users



You should have a similar landing page indicating that you are using the ArcGIS online under the UCSB license. You may need to authenticate with DUO on your phone.

title: I want to make a map
text:
Tour of the user interface
The main organization page lists the campus administrative contacts and open data groups available on campus. You can also see the latest content published by users on your campus.
Along the top of the page is the main toolbar.






Figure 3: ArcGIS Online main menu bar




Home will take you to the main landing page when you first sign in.
The Gallery contains items from our ‘featured content’ group
Groups are a list of groups which you can create or join. Some are invitation only. These are popular when you are working in group projects. For this workshop, we have created a group called From Maps to Analysis which contains most of the data layers we will be using.
Content is where your created or uploaded content is listed. You can make folders in here to organize your layers and features.
Notebooks is ESRI’s version of a JupyterHub-like environment. You can use ArcPy here. This may not be available to you based on your user role.
Organization will take you back to our main page. This is not the same as Home.
Scene, or Scene Viewer is where you can create 3D GIS scenes, such as neighborhood models and digital twins.
Map, or Map Viewer is where you can create 2D maps. We will be focusing on using the Map Viewer for this workshop.

title: I want to make a map
text:
Main Map components
In the Map Viewer there is a menu bar in the left column. This is where you can add components to your map. The way to think about a map is that it is made of different layers that are added on top of each other. Each layer adds specific information to your map. In our example, we will have a layer for the bike paths, one for the bike racks, one for the buildings, and so on… The base layer is special and often made of an image (but does not have to be). It is called a basemap. Here are the main components of your map:

Basemap: there are many provided by ArcGIS Online
Layers: your own and/or those shared by others
Legend: The symbology used on your map
Save and open...: Where you save your content

title: I want to make a map
text:
Basemap
The goal of a basemap is to provide context in terms of location and/or theme. In ArcGIS Online, a new map will always open with a basemap. Esri has about 20 different basemaps available. We will start with the default: the Topographic basemap.






Figure 5: Default basemap



In general, make sure you choose a basemap that is easy to follow and accurate in relation to the goal of your map. Avoid using busy basemaps that provide information not relevant to the purpose of your map. Additionally, choose a basemap that does not visually conflict with or override the layers on top. The message of your map is whatever you layer and annotate on top of the basemap; the basemap is there only to provide context.

title: I want to make a map
text:
Feature layers
Feature layers are the layers you add on top of your basemap. They are the main information your map is aiming at communicating. In ArcGIS, when you add an existing layer to your map, it will show up under your Layers. When you want to see the layer properties, you can either use the menu on the right hand column to view its properties or use the ... (we call this a “meatball” menu) next to the layer to open the same panel.

title: I want to make a map
section: Save your work - Save early, save often
text:
Save your work - Save early, save often






Figure 6: Open your menu bar to find the Save and open icon




There will be a blue dot next to the save icon until you save
You can organize all of your content into folders – Let’s make a folder for all of our work today. bike_map_workshop
Once you save, more options will be available
ArcGIS Online will not auto-save your map

title: I want to make a map
section: Step 1: Add layers to your map
text:
Step 1: Add layers to your map

Import lines Feature layer (bike paths)
From the Layers panel, click on the add layer button. Search My organization for UCSB neighborhood paths and roads. There should be only one result.




  



Figure 7: Adding a layer









TipChallenge: Repeat the above steps to add the feature layer UCSB Bike Racks to your map.





Import points layer (bike racks)






Figure 8: Add UCSB bike racks layer












TipChallenge: Find the ‘From Maps to Analysis’ group and add the UCSB Campus Buildings 2026 layer from there.





Add a layer via Groups






Figure 9: Add UCSB buildings layer








Reorder layers
After importing the three layers, you’ll notice they might not display optimally. There’s a GIS convention for layer ordering that helps ensure all features remain visible:
Layer Order Convention (top to bottom):

Points (e.g., bike racks) - should be on top
Lines (e.g., bike paths) - in the middle
Polygons (e.g., buildings) - at the bottom

This ordering ensures that smaller features aren’t hidden beneath larger polygon areas.
For our map, the recommended order from top to bottom should be:

UCSB Bike Racks (top)
UCSB neighborhood paths and roads (middle)
UCSB Campus Buildings 2026 (bottom)

To reorder the layers, click and hold on a layer name in the Layers panel, drag it to the desired position, and release.




  



Figure 10: Reorder feature layers





Accessing the underlying data
Feature layers are driven by data. Each point, line, or polygon has associated with it a row in an attribute table providing information on that specific record.
For example, if you click on the three dots on the right of a feature layer you can access its attribute table by selecting Show table.






Figure 11: Attribute table of UCSB buildings layer



In ArcGIS Online feature layers, we can understand the relationship between rows, columns, and features as follows:

Each row represents a feature: A row (record) corresponds to an individual spatial object on the map, such as a specific bike rack, a segment of a bike path, or a building.
Each column represents an attribute: Each column (field) corresponds to one specific attribute category or field name, such as the name of a building, the type of bike rack, or the length of a bike path. The value in each cell represents the specific attribute for that feature.

Your data can be visualized, selected, or analysed based on the columns of the attribute table. We will see later how you can leverage these attributes to set the symbology of a layer according to categories or quantities that are in the attribute table. You can also compute new attributes either based on other attributes or by performing analysis with other layers’ information. We will cover analysis tools in our second workshop.






NoteSave often.





Now that you have added the layers to your map, it’s a good idea to save it again.






Figure 12: Save as dialog in ArcGIS Online



In there, you can add a title, tags, and a short description of your map.

title: I want to make a map
text:
Step 2: Customize symbology & transparency
After adding our three layers, we have some work to do to make the map more readable. Let’s begin by adjusting the visibility of the UCSB Bike Racks layer. Currently, each bike rack is represented by a blue circle, which makes it difficult to identify the number of bike racks in a given area. We can use the aggregation feature to group the bike racks into dynamic clusters, which will facilitate the visualization of the number of bike racks in a given area. This feature will automatically group the bike racks into clusters based on the map scale, so that when you zoom in, the clusters will break apart into individual bike racks.
To enable aggregation, follow these steps:

Click on the layer UCSB Bike Racks to open its properties panel.
On the right side panel, click on the Aggregation button (the fifth button from the top).
In the Aggregation panel, select the Clustering option. This will enable the clustering of bike racks based on the map scale.







Figure 13: Enabling aggregation for the bike racks layer



We can also adjust the transparency of the circles representing the bike racks to smooth the circle overlap. To do this, follow these steps:

Click on the layer UCSB Bike Racks to open its properties panel.
On the right side panel, click on the Styles button (the second button from the top).
In the Styles panel, go to the Pick a style section, and click on the Style options button.
In the Style options panel, click on the edit button (the pencil icon) next to the symbol in the Symbol style list.
In the Symbol style panel, set the Fill transparency to 30%. Changes will be applied immediately to the map.







Figure 14: Adjusting the transparency of the bike racks layer



To have a better view of the bike racks area, click on the three dots next to the UCSB Bike Racks layer and select Zoom to layer. This will zoom in to the extent of the bike racks layer.






Figure 15: Zooming to the extent of the bike racks layer




Adjust style based on attribute
Our map is starting to look good, but you can notice that the buildings are all filled with the same color (orange in our case). Although the buildings are not the main focus of our map, this layer can be useful to provide context, so we can adjust the symbology to make it more informative.
To achieve this, we can adjust the symbology of the UCSB Campus Buildings 2026 layer based on an attribute. Our first step is to identify the attribute we want to use. We can open the layer attribute table as we previously showed, or we can see the available attributes directly from the Styles panel. To do this, follow these steps:

Click on the layer UCSB Campus Buildings 2026 to open its properties panel.
On the right side panel, click on the Styles button (the second button from the top).
In the Styles panel, go to the Choose attributes section, and click on the + Field button. This will show you the available attributes for this layer.







Figure 16: List of available attributes for the UCSB Campus Buildings 2026 layer



To explore the values of the attributes, you can click on the (i) icon next to the attribute name. This will show you the metadata for that attribute and a list with its top 10 values.
For this exercise, we will use the BLDGTYPE attribute, which represents the building type (e.g., housing, academic and administrative, recreation, parking, etc.). This attribute will allow us to fill each building with a different color based on its use.

Check the box next to the BLDGTYPE attribute and click on the Add button. This will add the attribute to the Choose attributes section, and set a predefined color ramp to fill the building areas based on their use.







Figure 17: Adding the BLDGTYPE attribute to the Styles panel



We can select a color ramp that better fits our map:

In the Styles panel, click on the Style options button in Types (unique symbols) section.
Click on the edit button (the pencil icon) next to the color ramp in the Symbol style list.
In the Symbol style panel, click on the edit button (the pencil icon) next to the color ramp in the Colors section.
Select the Stone and Gravel color ramp. Changes will be applied immediately to the map.







Figure 18: Changing the color ramp for the BLDGTYPE attribute



In this specific layer we also have a category with no label and zero records. We can remove this category by clicking the check box next to it and selecting Remove from the contextual menu.






Figure 19: Removing the empty category from the BLDGTYPE attribute





Filter layer based on attribute
Finally, we are interested in displaying bike paths from the UCSB neighborhood paths and roads layer that also contains roads, pathways and other features. We can filter the categories we are interested in using the filter function on the right sidebar.

Click on the layer UCSB neighborhood paths and roads to select it.
Click on the Filter button on the right sidebar (third from top).






Figure 20: Adding a filter to the road layer



Click Add new
In the condition box, choose the highway field and the includes condition, and select cycleway
Don’t forget to save with the button at the bottom!







Figure 21: Filtering out the bike paths



Because bike paths are relevant to our map, we can change the color to make them stand out more. To do this we can change the symbol color to a warm, earthy ochre color that contrasts with the blue of the bike racks and colors of the basemap.

Click on the layer UCSB neighborhood paths and roads to select it.
Click on the Styles button on the right sidebar (second from top).
In the Styles panel, click on the Style options button in Types (unique symbols) section.
Click on the edit button (the pencil icon) next to the symbol in the Symbol style list.
In the Symbol style panel, click on the color box and type in the hex code d67d1e for the ochre color.







Figure 22: Changing the color of the bike paths




Change the width of the line to 2 px to match the width of the basemap roads.







Figure 23: Changing the width of the bike paths









NoteSave often.





Now that you have customized the symbology of your layers, it’s a good idea to save your map again.






Figure 24: Save as dialog in ArcGIS Online



In there, you can add a title, tags, and a short description of your map.





Select a different basemap
After adding the layers and customizing their symbology, we have a good, almost ready map. However, the current basemap (Topographic) is a bit too busy and makes it hard to see the features we added. Let’s change it to a different basemap using the Basemap option in the left menu bar.






Figure 25: Basemap option in the left menu bar



From the basemap gallery, we can select another basemap. In our case, we will select the Terrain with Labels basemap, which is a lighter version of the Topographic basemap. This will make our features stand out more and make the map easier to read.






Figure 26: Map with Terrain with Labels basemap



Don’t forget to save your map after making these changes!

title: I want to make a map
text:
Step 3: Annotate the map
In addition to bringing in structured geospatial data layers, maps are often used to sketch ideas, mock up proposals, or add contextual annotations. This is a common practice in urban planning and design.
We can add these annotations by creating a sketch layer. Unlike feature layers, sketch layers are designed for drawing shapes (points, lines, polygons, circles, text) directly onto the map as descriptive elements. Sketch layers differ from feature layers in a few other ways as well:

Sketch layers can contain different kinds of geometries (points, lines, polygons), while feature layers are typically constrained to a single geometry type.
Sketch layers are part of the map, and stored in the map, while feature layers are independent objects that are stored separately and which the map references.
Sketch layer shapes do not have attributes, and sketch layers do not have attribute tables.
Sketch layers do not appear in the map legend.







Figure 27: Sketch layer option in the left menu



After adding the sketch layer to your workspace, a new menu will appear in the right column with drawing tools and configuration options.






Figure 28: Sketch layer drawing tools menu




The Campus Access Proposal
Imagine you are a campus active transportation planner. Your goal is to propose an infrastructure upgrade that connects an existing bike path to a campus building with high bike-parking density (visible from your UCSB Bike Racks and UCSB Campus Buildings 2026 layers) where no direct bike path currently exists.
To present your proposal, you will add exactly two sketches to your map: a proposed connecting path and a safety dismount zone.


1. Proposed Path Connector (Line)
Find a major campus building that is near a bike path but lacks a direct bike-lane connection to its entrance or bike racks.

Select the line drawing tool from the sketch layer menu.
Click on an existing bike path to start drawing your proposed route, click to add vertices (turns) along pedestrian pathways or open spaces, and double-click to finish the line at the building’s entrance plaza.

Customize the line symbol in the sketch layer menu to make it look like a planning proposal:

Width: 2 px
Pattern: Dotted or Dashed
Color: Light Blue (#5aaac4) or an eye-catching accent color of your choice.





  



Figure 29: Drawing a proposed route line on the map





2. Pedestrian Safety Dismount Zone (Circle or Polygon)
Because your proposed path ends at a busy building entrance, we need to designate a safety buffer zone where bicyclists must dismount to prevent conflicts with pedestrians entering and exiting the building.

Select the circle drawing tool (or polygon tool) from the sketch layer menu.
Click and drag near the building entrance to create a buffer zone covering the plaza where the new path terminates.
Click on the select tool to finish the shape.

Customize the zone to look like a semi-transparent advisory overlay:

Fill color: Red (#d13434) or Orange
Fill transparency: 40% (allowing the underlying basemap and buildings to remain visible)
Outline: Thin solid line or no outline





  



Figure 30: Drawing a dismount zone circle on the map




Finally, rename your sketch layer to Proposed Improvements to reflect its purpose. Click on the three dots next to the sketch layer, select Rename, enter the new name, and click OK.
Save your map after making these changes!

title: I want to make a map
section: Step 4: Prepare the map for publication
text:
Step 4: Prepare the map for publication
Almost there! At this point you’re ready to start packaging your map for publication.
To do that, you need to look for the Print option in the left menu bar.






Figure 31: Print option in the left menu bar



For exporting the map you have two options:

Layout: This option allows you to create a more complex layout with additional map elements such as title, legend, scale bar, north arrow, etc. You can choose from several pre-defined templates or create your own custom layout.
Map only: With this option, you can export just the map itself without any additional elements. You can choose the file format (PNG, PDF, etc.) and the resolution of the exported map.

For our purposes, we will select the Layout option to create a more complete map for publication.
In the layout menu, you can change the title of the map, select a Template (which is basically a standard page size and orientation), and select the File format for the export (e.g., PNG, PDF).
You can also customize the layout further by enabling the Advanced options panel. You can set the scale, add an author name, include copyright information, increase or decrease the resolution, indicate the output spatial reference, and select to include legend, north arrow, and scale bar.
Adjust the zoom and position of the map in the preview window to ensure everything is visible and well-framed.






TipMap resolution



If your map is intended for print publication, it is recommended that you set your DPI value to 300 dpi. For web or screen display, 96 dpi is generally sufficient and will produce a smaller file size.








Figure 32: Map export layout configuration panel

title: I want to make a map
text:
Step 5: Share your map
When you’re satisfied with the layout and settings, click on the Export button to generate the map. Depending on the selected file format and resolution, it may take a few moments to process the export.
The result will be listed in the Exports panel, where you can save the file to your computer by clicking on the three dots next to the export and selecting Save as.






Figure 33: Saving exported map from the Exports panel



This will save the exported map to your ArcGIS Online content. You can access it later from the Content menu in the top menu bar. The new item will be available as an Image file that you can download to your computer.






Figure 34: Downloading the exported map image from ArcGIS Online content









WarningPublic sharing





You can share your map publicly and embed it on a website, just like we did at the beginning of this lesson. However, for this to work, you need to set the visibility of all your map layers to public.

title: I want to make a map
section: Preview for Workshop 2: Working with data
text:
Preview for Workshop 2: Working with data
In Workshop 2, we dive deeper into managing and manipulating various types of geospatial data in ArcGIS online. Building on our biking project from Workshop 1, we will combine terrain data with local trailhead locations to analyze trail accessibility by bike.
In this second session, you will learn to:

Understand the vector and raster geospatial data types
Import external data into ArcGIS Online
Create, edit, and update data of feature layers
Export processed data from ArcGIS Online back to your local machine

title: I want to make a map
text:
Other approaches
There are many ways of making a simple map. Here are some alternative approaches.

By screen grabbing: Create a base layer by screen grabbing a source map displayed in a web browser window (e.g., Google Maps). Then, using a drawing tool (a dedicated drawing tool such as Adobe Illustrator, or any program that provides drawing tools such as Microsoft PowerPoint), import the screen grab and draw on top of that. It is possible to capture the base layer at higher-than-screen resolution by zooming in, panning and screen grabbing it in pieces, and merging the pieces using a tool like Adobe Photoshop. And by measuring distances between known points, and/or carefully keeping track of scale, it is possible to accurately position figures and annotations.
Google Earth: An in-browser tool that allows you to view and add data layers with high-resolution Google imagery. There are some fee based services in Google Earth, and you may need a plan to view some features. Historical satellite imagery is available.
Mapbox: Mapbox has more features available for mobile users. Maps can be viewed and edited on mobile devices.
OpenStreetMap: OpenStreetMap is open source and managed and created by users worldwide. This data can also be downloaded and added to GIS software like ArcGIS Pro or QGIS.
CalTopo comes with a variety of base layers, including multiple types of topographic maps, and it provides a number of drawing and annotation tools. Certain features may require a subscription.

title: I want to make a map
text:
Caveats of using ArcGIS Online
Two central concepts of open science are reproducibility, by which we mean the ability to inspect (if not re-execute or replicate) all the data sources, code, protocols, and other materials used in a study, and citation, the ability to persistently and openly refer to and access those same data sources, code, protocols, and other materials. Unfortunately, a proprietary, closed tool like ArcGIS Online fails to support open science in three important ways.

The artifacts one works with in ArcGIS Online (layers, maps, StoryMaps, etc.) are stored internally and inaccessibly in an unknown, proprietary format. The data can be viewed or otherwise accessed through ArcGIS Online to be sure, and perhaps edited if one has a paid subscription, but the data in its raw form is inaccessible.
The storage, commitment to persistence, and access costs of artifacts stored in ArcGIS Online are entirely dependent on a commercial company.
Artifacts such as maps can be identified by URLs, but not by the DOI identifiers that are commonplace in scholarly communication, and which are often required by publishers, citation tracking systems, and academic promotion committees.

An additional caveat that applies to all UI-based GIS tools, not just ArcGIS Online, is that operations are performed interactively. Unfortunately, interactive use does not create any kind of historical log of actions performed. While this style of interface allows for free and fast exploration, it comes at the cost of being able to reliably re-create processing steps. Notice in this workshop that the sequence of actions used to create your map are not recorded anywhere. For a map this may not matter, nor may it matter for a one-off analysis, but if you wanted to, say, apply the same set of steps to a new map, or if your work within ArcGIS Online involved spatial analysis, it will likely be critical that the processing steps be recorded in such a way that they can be inspected if not re-run.
ArcGIS Online is a powerful tool, to be sure. But to use it in a way that supports open, reproducible science, we recommend that you:

Export newly-created feature layers as Shapefiles, and/or export attributes tables as CSV files, and make those files preserved and citable by storing them in a data repository. Do not consider ArcGIS Online to be any kind of long-term repository.
Express significant computations programmatically, so that they can be inspected and re-run.

text:
Review: Annotations vs. Data
In Workshop 1, we started with sketch layers to draw points, lines, and polygons directly on top of the map. While sketches are convenient for quick markups and annotations, they are not true GIS data layers. Sketches lack an underlying database table and cannot be queried, filtered, or used in spatial analysis.
In contrast, feature layers link geometries (points, lines, or polygons) to structured records in an attribute table. Each feature has defined attributes, or fields (e.g., name, speed limit, road type, elevation) with specific data types (such as text strings, numbers, and dates). This tabular structure makes it possible to filter features, symbolize data based on its attributes, and calculate spatial relationships.

title: Working with Data
text:
Raster vs Vector Data
Geographic data generally falls into two primary models: vector and raster.



The difference in geospatial work is the same as between Adobe Illustrator (vectors) and Photoshop (rasters) (image credit: Graphic Mama



Vector Data
So far we have only looked at vector data. Vector data represents discrete geographic features using coordinate geometry:

Points: Single \((X, Y)\) coordinate pairs representing discrete locations (e.g., bike racks, bus stops, accident locations).
Lines (Polylines): Ordered sequences of vertices connecting locations to represent linear features or networks (e.g., bike paths, roads, transit routes, streams).
Polygons: Closed shapes enclosing an area defined by connected coordinate vertices (e.g., campus buildings, land parcels, parks, water bodies).

Every shape is tied to a row in an attribute table, where each column holds specific properties describing that feature. For example, if we pop open the table and look at the attributes for the “Library” building,
First selecting the polygon Library 
Then opening the Attribute Table under layer options by clicking the ... 
Each polygon in the table has many fields and values associated with it. Building names, floor counts, area, who edited the file, and when it was last updated, among other fields a user may find helpful when analyzing their data.
Attributes may be divided into three types:

Nominal: information with labels and names - building type
Numerical: information that can be counted or has numerical importance - shape area
Ordinal: information that can be ordered or ranked in some way - floor count



Raster Data
Raster data represents the landscape as a regular grid of square cells (pixels) organized into rows and columns.

Single-band rasters: Each pixel contains a single numerical value representing a continuous measurement (such as elevation in a Digital Elevation Model [DEM], slope, or temperature) or an integer code representing a category (such as land cover types).
Multi-band rasters: Each pixel contains multiple values across different spectral channels or bands (such as red, green, blue, and near-infrared bands in aerial photography or satellite imagery).

Below is a single band raster. The value of each pixel is elevation.

Below is an 8-band raster with band #7 (near IR) as red, band #3 (green) as green, and band #1 (coastal blue) as blue. This type of image displays are often called “false-color” because they do not respect the RGB channel alignment. This can help to highlight some features, such as vegetation that has a strong signal in near infrared (NIR) wavelengths



The Story So Far
In the first workshop, we created a bicycle map of campus and Isla Vista using pre-existing data.
Our goal for part 2 is to plan a challenging and comfortable bicycle route that leads from the UCSB campus into the surrounding Goleta community and the Santa Ynez foothills. And we want to put our bike on the bus on the way back. To accomplish this, we need to expand beyond campus bike paths and incorporate regional road networks; we want to look at elevation data to look for steep climbs and long views; and we need to find those bus stops.

title: Working with Data
text:
Exploring Raster Data
When outside of ArcGIS Online, geospatial raster data comes in many different formats. TIFFs, Grids, netCDF, iiif, web map services. Too many to list!

ArcGIS Online variations: while many of these start somewhere as TIFFs, they are all ingested into AGO as flavors of Tiled imagery layers

Let’s add a Digital Elevation Model to out map: ucsb_local_dem. By default, a single channel or one band raster is displayed as grayscale, with low values black and high values white.
Your map with DEM should look something like this by default:



Digital Elevation Model added to the map


Each pixel, or cell, in our DEM represents bare-earth surface elevation relative to a vertical datum (mean sea level). The ucsb_local_dem dataset was derived from a high-resolution USGS LiDAR survey (3D Elevation Program (3DEP)).
POP QUIZ: What do you think are the units of ucsb_local_dem?
A DEM is an example of a continuous raster as the values stored in each cell correspond to a quantity gradient (elevation in meters) changing in space . Other examples of continuous raster would be precipitation measurements, air quality index, ocean salinity, or distance from a road.
In the layer properties, explore the raster statistics: note the minimum elevation near sea level (0) along the coast and slough, rising to hundreds of feet in the foothills, as well as the grid cell resolution.






TipChallenge: Does our DEM contain negative values? Why?





yes. because sea level.
** screenshot here **
To do: put in screenshot with properties here. The properties table shows the maximum and minimum values




Applying a Divergent Color Scheme
Data that moves around a zero point, such as our batho-topo elevation model, is knows as ** divergent **. It is very helpful to your map viewers to visualize this typ of data with a divergent color scheme.
By default, continuous raster layers display using a grayscale “Stretch” renderer (low values ‘0’ dark, and high values 255 light). To clearly distinguish elevation changes across the coastal plain and mountains, let’s change the symbology to a continuous, diverging color ramp (e.g., a below-and-above zero diverging ramp or an elevation palette). Select the DEM layer and open the Styles menu ()
to use ‘Stretch’, we have to force zero to be the middle value. When we need to do this, we look at the DEM’s actual minimum and maximum values, and take whichever number has the larger absolute value. Use that exact number as both a negative minimum and a positive maximum in the Statistics table. (e.g.: 1218 feet)

Here is below an example of a widely used color scale for DEM, with lower elevation display in blue and green and higher elevation in brown and white.
{fig-alt=“Digital Elevation Model with color scaled for DEM: white a higher elevation, blue and green for lower elevation” scale](images/workshop2/w2_dem_colored.png){fig-alt=“Digital Elevation Model with color scaled for DEM: white a higer elevation, blue and green for lower elevation” width=“90%” fig-align=“center”}


‘Binning’ a raster
It’s sometimes easier to divide a raster into classes. You can do this on the fly in ArcGIS Online by changing the symbology
….


Calculated Raster Data: Slope
You can also perform calculations to turn a DEM into a slope layer. We already made this slope layer for you as it can be a computing intensive task. This is another continuous dataset. You can call it derivative data.
We will learn how it was made in workshop 3, but for now we will use it to examine, with our eyes, where the steepest bike routes up into our foothills are. Add this raster layer by searching for SantaBarbara_slope within the UCSB organization:

POP QUIZ: Below same slope layer, zoomed in to campus, and symbolized with a divergent color scheme. What does this tell you is incorrect about something we said earlier regarding our DEM? (DTM vs DSM)

Resymbolize your slope layer to a color scheme that makes sense to you. Look up into the foothills. Which paths look steepest for our theoretical bike ride?



Categorical Rasters - Land Cover
Categorical vs. Continuous Data
Continuous data are best represented by numbers, and are logically consistent when you do so. Smaller numbers = less of some measurement.
On the other hand, categorical data can be text or numeric. The value of any numbers used do not necessarily reflect any mathematical value, but it may. For example, while the values below have a natural order (The 3 Little Piggies Construction Scale), the numbers are ordinal but arbitrary:

1 = reinforced concrete or steel beam
2 = wood stick construction
3 = baked brick masonry
4 = adobe
5 = sun brick / mud daub
6 = straw bail

While elevation is a continuous raster (values change smoothly along a numerical gradient representing a quantity), other rasters are categorical rasters (e.g., land cover classification datasets from the Living Atlas, where integer cell values represent categories such as urban development, forest, or water).

Show the legend to see the category names. Open the attribute table to compare it to what appears for vector data:


Multi-band Rasters
So far we have worked with single-channel, or 1-band rasters. However, perhaps we are more familiar with 3-channel images, because our eyes see best in the red-green-blue color space. For geospatial data, think of this as satellite or aerial views.
For digital images, 3 ‘bands’ of wavelengths are stored separately. When the computer combines them together, we humans see something akin to what we see when we look at nature with our eyes. However, we can swap in other bandwidths of radiation, such as near infrared, or microwave, and see completely other things.
The DREAM Lab hosts several satellite views of campus created by Planet Labs, a private satellite firm. Its fleet of PlanetScope satellites captures imagery in 8 bandwidth divisions of the electromagnetic spectrum. 8-band images. Let’s add one of those layers now:

Uploading a raster image to ArcGIS Online takes up storage, so we aren’t going to do that. However we can also add vector and tabular data to our map!

Creating Vector Layers from .CSV files
In this section we will import SantaBarbara_County_Trailheads.csv from a CSV spreadsheet using coordinate columns (latitude and longitude) to see how external tabular data can be transformed into a geospatial layer and integrate with existing road and elevation layers.
Download and open the SantaBarbara_County_Trailheads.csv onto your device.

Which attributes are storing the geospatial information?
What is the quality of this dataset? Anything suspect?





CSV import wizard

Add layer from file



Select “Your Device” and browse to the csv file you want to import



Leave the default option “Create a hosted feature layer and add it to the map” and click Next



Select the attributes you would like to import as well as rename fields as you see necessary. You can also use this step to rename any of the field. Let’s select all the fields up to “Overview” and Rename “Title” as “Name”. It is also a good practice to check that the field types are aligned with what you were expecting.



Match the latitude and longitude information used by ArcGIS to generate the location with your data attributes.



Save your new data layer under your user account creating a ucsb_bike folder if you have not one yet



Zoom out to see the trailhead locations! Of course now we need to make it look better :)








NoteCRS





A note on Coordinate Reference Systems
In ArcGIS Online, the default projection and Coordinate Reference System (CRS) is WGS 1984 Web Mercator Auxiliary Sphere, also used by the Global Positioning System (GPS).
Coordinate systems can be divided into two main categories: Projected and Geographic Coordinate Systems.

Projected Coordinate Systems use a 2D flat surface to define locations and is measured in linear units. Locations are identified by x,y coordinates
Geographic Coordinate Systems use a 3D spherical surface measured in angular units to define locations on earth. A point is referred by its latitude and longitude.

There are plethora of CRSs that all have different accuracy and other advantages depending on your location and extent of your area of interest. Here is a good website to look at the different CRSs: https://epsg.io/

Choose a good color ramp, e.g. green-yellow for easy-moderate and red-purple for difficult
Increase the point size to 12px
Give a title to the legend “Trail difficulty”

title: Working with Data
text:
Editing Feature Layers
Now that we have imported data into ArcGIS, we might also want to modify this data. For vector data, we can modify attributes and values stored in the underlying table or the feature itself by editing locations and shapes, or adding and removing specific features. For raster data, those transformations are generally done using some form of calculation on the entire raster, or specific values targeted via conditions, rather than by manually editing pixel values. We will talk more about raster calculations in our third workshop. For today, we will focus on editing vector data (or feature layers in ArcGIS jargon) in this workshop.






WarningThis goes beyond the map





It is important to understand that when we are editing a feature layer, it is independent of the map. You are actually changing the data stored under your content.
This also means that you might not have the right to edit some of the data you are using in your map because you do not own them! A potential workaround is to create a local copy of the data, but some data provider do not allow this either.




Editing Features
We noticed that some locations of trailhead on the Goleta Beach Park, east of campus, are in the ocean. This is probably due to some imprecision of the GPS measurements. We thus want to move those points back to the beach



Trailheads in ocean (red dots) that we would like to move back to the shore (sand dots)


To edit a feature layer, need:

To make sure that the layer is selected (name in bold) in the layer panel on the left
In the toolbar on the right, click on the edit icon  to start the edit mode

This should open the Editor panel on the right of your map



Feature layer Editor panel


The top part (in red) of this panel lets you edit the feature layer elements. Below, you can add new features to existing layers (for our trailhead layer in magenta).
Since we want to move our trailhead locations individually, we can use the Select by point tool (next to the hand) to:

Select a point of interest by clicking on it.







Once selected, the dot should have a cyan halo around it and you should see its values for the attributes on the right.







Then drag the point to the new location, close by the building.
Confirm the change, by clicking on the blue “Update” button at the bottom of the panel.






You have edited the layer! Note that if it is a layer used in multiple maps (by you or others you have shared it with), all the maps will be updated as well, because remember maps and layers are two separate entities.






TipChallenge - Move the other point to the beach!











Adding a New Feature
Looking around UCSB campus location, we realized that there is no point for the campus lagoon trail!! Let’s add it to the map. We will decide that the trail starts next to the marine lab.
To add a point to our trailhead layer:

Click on New Feature in the edit panel for this layer
Your cursor should become a cross, click on the map to place your point
Fill out the information for this new point (leave lat/long blank)
Hit “Create” to add your new feature to the layer






Make sure to get out of the Create features mode before clicking again on the map!






Note





Note that the geospatial information used by ArcGIS online to display the point is not store in the attribute table. This is why the Latitude and Longitude values could be left blank and the point still being displayed!





Editing the Attribute Table
You can also edit the information underlying the data by directly modifying the table. You can add/remove attributes as well as directly editing the values.

Adding an attribute
Now that we have added a new trailhead, we might want to add a new attribute that will let us track if a specific point is from the original dataset or something that we have added. You can add an attribute using the Field tool on the right . This should open a new panel listing all the current fields and at the button you should see an + Add field button.

Click on it
Choose “Numeric” -> “Integer” & click “Next”
Enter the following values & click “Add field”

 Now you should have the “Added” field listed in the field list on the right panel.


Editing values
Let’s open the table to have a look at the values.
The new field has been added as the last column. The point we created should be at the bottom of the table, as the last row.
There are two ways to edit values in a table. You can double-click on a cell and change the values, or you can use the pen logo at the end of the rows that will open back the “Edit Feature” pane we used previously. Let’s directly modify the values by double-clicking in the new “Added” column and setting the value to 1. Also notice that the other “Distance” values all have a unit, let’s add Miles to the 1.5 we entered previously.



Attribute table with the newly entered values


Of course, there are more advanced ways to edit values than cell by cell. One of them is using the filed calculator that let’s you use expressions (conditions, formulas, …) to calculate values of a field. We do not have time to tackle this topic today, But see here for more information on how to do this.

text:
Exporting Data
At some point in your analysis, you might want to also download the data in addition to your map, for example, to move to a scripted environment such as R and Python to conduct statistical analysis. This is a multi-step process: first, you will have to export the feature layer in a downloadable format; then you will be able to download this layer to your local computer.
You can not export a layer from the Map Viewer, you will need to first return to the “My Content” view. You can do this by using the “Burger” menu at the top-left of your Map view and selecting Content.

Once in the My content view, locate and click on the spatial trailhead layer you imported from the CSV file to go to the Overview page of that layer.



Unfold the menu on the right completely, select Export data, and choose the GeoJSON format.



On the next window, leave the default options and choose your ucsb_bike folder as location. Click on Export. Note that exporting data can take some time, so be patient :)



Once the export is completed, you should automatically be redirected to the Overview page of this new dataset. This time, Download should be available in the menu on the right side of the page. Click on it and select a location on your local computer and a filename.

title: Working with Data
text:
How to improve your map

Creating Shaded Relief (Hillshade) on the Fly
One use for a DEM is to make a shaded relief layer. That is a classic view that gives the terrain realistic three-dimensional depth and surface texture, we can generate a shaded relief visualization dynamically:

Duplicate the ucsb_local_dem layer.
Rename the two DEM layers for clarity: name the top layer Elevation (Color) and the bottom layer Elevation (Shaded Relief).
Change the symbology style to Shaded Relief.

Shaded relief simulates how sunlight illuminates terrain, casting shadows based on the position of the sun measured as two angles: Azimuth and Altitude

Azimuth: The compass direction from which the illumination source (the sun) originates, measured in degrees clockwise from north (0° = North, 90° = East, 180° = South, 270° = West). In cartography, the sun is traditionally positioned in the northwest (315°) or west (270°) to match how the human brain interprets light and shadow, preventing an optical illusion known as “relief inversion” where mountains appear as valleys. For our map, we position the light source from the west.
Altitude: The angle of the sun above the horizon, measured from 0° (level with the horizon at sunrise/sunset) to 90° (directly overhead at solar noon). A lower altitude (e.g., 30°–45°, typical of low winter sun) produces longer, more dramatic shadows that accentuate ridge lines, canyons, and valleys.


We can adjust those angles to show the sun in the morning or evening here in Santa Barbara.
Adjust the transparency of the top colored elevation layer so the shaded relief beneath shows through, creating an illuminated 3D terrain effect under our roads.



Current status of our map with colored DEM and shaded relief


This matches interim map 3 in our group.
This is a bit of an artificial example, because Esri offers a wide variety of hillshade basemaps in the Living Atlas. Also: that was a rather lengthy aside.
Now would be an excellent point to save your map.

section: Preview for Workshop 3: Looking Ahead to Spatial Analysis
text:
Preview for Workshop 3: Looking Ahead to Spatial Analysis
In Workshop 3, we dive deeper into quantitative spatial analysis. The data layers we prepared today form the foundation for analyzing terrain and route difficulty:
- Calculate slope from the DEM (a single-channel continuous raster measuring steepness)
- Overlay slope values onto road segments
- Identify and highlight the steepest climbs (maximum slope)

Analysis Workflow Overview

Slope Calculation: Use raster analysis tools to calculate a slope raster from the DEM, expressing terrain steepness in degrees or percent rise.
Zonal Statistics as Table: With the slope raster and the road network loaded, run Raster Analysis > Zonal Statistics as Table to compute summary statistics (such as the maximum or mean slope) for each road line.



Joining Statistics to Roads: The zonal statistics tool outputs a standalone data table. To visualize these slope measurements on the map, join the table back to the road vector layer using Tools > Summarize data > Join Features, matching on a common identifier such as OBJECTID.



Once joined, roads can be symbolized by slope steepness, allowing us to pinpoint the steepest hill climbs for our ride!
